explanation: King Sejong's scholars created it in the 1440s so ordinary people could learn to read. Some consonant shapes sketch the mouth, tongue or throat making each sound.

claims.text: Korean is written in the Hangul alphabet.
Hiragana and katakana are Japanese scripts, and Devanagari is used for Hindi and other languages of India and Nepal.
Hangul was created under King Sejong in the 1440s, partly so that ordinary people could learn to read and write.
The shapes of several basic Hangul consonants represent the position of the mouth, tongue or throat when the sound is made.

evidence.restatement: Hiragana and katakana are Japanese scripts, and Devanagari writes Hindi, Nepali, Marathi and other languages.
King Sejong and his scholars created Hangul in 1443 and promulgated it in 1446, so that common people could learn to read and write.

claimResults.note: High-risk: knowledge only, so it counts only once a confirming check carries dataset or web evidence (§9.9 rule 3). No pinned dataset states it, and this run had no WebSearch: the shared per-turn search budget was exhausted before its first search ran.

evidence.restatement: The basic consonant letters picture the speech organs, such as the tongue tip against the gum ridge for n and the tongue root closing the throat for g.
Korean is written in Hangul (hanja, Chinese characters, survive only in limited use).
Hiragana and katakana are Japanese kana; Devanagari writes Hindi, Nepali and other languages.
Hangul was devised under King Sejong in the 1440s (completed 1443, proclaimed 1446) so ordinary people could read and write.
Several basic Hangul consonant shapes model the speech organs: the mouth, tongue or throat.
